arguments.name: Boater Preference Survey with Insurance Incentive
arguments.method: Online survey of recreational boaters in coastal states, presenting two product concepts: (1) a differentiated PLB marketed as a safety essential for remote boating, priced at $700; (2) the same PLB offered with a $200 insurance subsidy (effective price $500) and a statement that insurers may require it. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay. The survey also asks about current safety gear ownership and insurance status.
arguments.sample: 500 recreational boaters recruited via boating clubs and marine forums, stratified by state (California, Florida, Washington) to reflect high boater participation. Recruitment cost estimated €2,000.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent rate for the differentiated product (T1) vs. purchase intent rate when insurance subsidy is offered (T2). Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the differentiated product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be at least 10% for the differentiated product at $700, and will not increase significantly when a subsidy is offered (difference <5 percentage points).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will increase by at least 10 percentage points when the insurance subsidy is offered, indicating that price reduction and insurer involvement drive adoption.

arguments.decision_rule: If the purchase intent for the differentiated product at $700 is ≥10% AND the increase in intent when subsidy is offered is <5 percentage points, then T1 is supported and ACR should pursue a differentiated consumer proposition. If the increase is ≥10 percentage points, T2 is supported and ACR should explore insurance partnership. If neither condition is met, no expansion is recommended.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., personal marine safety beacon for recreational boaters).

X1.name: Channel Preference Test for Recreational Boaters
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios targeting US recreational boaters (self-identified owners of boats under 26 feet). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (1) Premium Retail Scenario: product described as a differentiated safety essential for remote boating, priced at $700, sold through specialty marine retailers; (2) Insurance Subsidy Scenario: same product described as meeting insurance requirements, priced at $500, with a note that insurance companies may subsidize or require it, sold through insurance brokers. Participants indicate (a) likelihood to purchase (1-10), (b) maximum price they would pay, and (c) whether they would recommend the product to peers. The survey also asks about current safety equipment ownership and insurance coverage.
X1.sample: 400 US recreational boaters recruited via boating forums and marine insurance newsletters, balanced between the two conditions (200 each).
X1.measure: Primary outcome: average likelihood to purchase (1-10) in each condition. Secondary outcomes: maximum price willingness, recommendation intent, and self-reported insurance coverage.

arguments.claim: Recreational boaters will adopt a differentiated 406 MHz PLB if it is marketed as a safety essential for remote water activities, because they value personal safety and are willing to pay a premium for a device that reliably alerts SAR.
arguments.who_benefits: ACR Electronics would benefit by capturing premium pricing and brand association with safety.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Boaters perceive the PLB as a critical safety device that reduces risk of drowning or injury in remote areas; regulatory approval (FCC) signals legitimacy and safety compliance.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price the PLB above standard marine electronics (e.g., $700) and sell through specialty marine retailers, earning higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Recreational boating market in the US is large enough to support a differentiated product.
Boaters are willing to allocate budget to safety equipment beyond basic requirements.
Specialty marine retailers will stock a differentiated PLB if it meets safety standards.
predictions: If ACR launches a differentiated PLB for recreational boaters, sales will be driven by safety-conscious buyers rather than price-sensitive bulk purchasers.
Surveyed boaters will indicate intent to purchase a PLB priced at $700 if it is marketed as a safety essential.
Retail partners will request the product for their safety equipment sections.

arguments.claim: Insurance companies will subsidize or require 406 MHz PLBs for recreational boaters, creating demand because they reduce claim costs and meet regulatory safety standards.
arguments.who_benefits: ACR Electronics would benefit by selling PLBs through insurance channels at volume, potentially at lower margins but higher total sales.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Insurance providers view PLBs as risk mitigation tools that lower the likelihood of costly rescue operations and claims; they may offer discounts or require PLB ownership as a condition of coverage.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can secure bulk contracts with insurers, selling PLBs at a modest margin but achieving higher volume and market penetration than premium retail sales.
assumptions: Insurance companies in the US marine market are willing to subsidize safety devices.
Regulatory or industry standards encourage PLB adoption for insured vessels.
Insurers have the authority to mandate or incentivize PLB ownership.
predictions: If ACR partners with insurers, PLB sales will be driven by policyholders rather than individual safety-conscious buyers.
Insurance companies will request PLBs at a price point below retail (e.g., $500) to pass savings to customers.
Policyholders will report PLB ownership as a condition of their insurance coverage.

arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that recreational boaters specifically seek or purchase PLBs, nor that they are willing to pay a premium price.

arguments.name: Channel Preference Test for Recreational Boaters
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios targeting US recreational boaters (self-identified owners of boats under 26 feet). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (1) Premium Retail Scenario: product described as a differentiated safety essential for remote boating, priced at $700, sold through specialty marine retailers; (2) Insurance Subsidy Scenario: same product described as meeting insurance requirements, priced at $500, with a note that insurance companies may subsidize or require it, sold through insurance brokers. Participants indicate (a) likelihood to purchase (1-10), (b) maximum price they would pay, and (c) whether they would recommend the product to peers. The survey also asks about current safety equipment ownership and insurance coverage.
arguments.sample: 400 US recreational boaters recruited via boating forums and marine insurance newsletters, balanced between the two conditions (200 each).
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: average likelihood to purchase (1-10) in each condition. Secondary outcomes: maximum price willingness, recommendation intent, and self-reported insurance coverage.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher likelihood to purchase and higher willingness to pay in the Premium Retail Scenario than in the Insurance Subsidy Scenario, because safety-conscious boaters value the differentiated safety proposition and are willing to pay a premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher likelihood to purchase and higher willingness to pay in the Insurance Subsidy Scenario than in the Premium Retail Scenario, because insurance-driven demand and subsidy reduce price sensitivity and create a mandatory purchase incentive.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average likelihood to purchase in the Premium Retail Scenario exceeds that in the Insurance Subsidy Scenario by at least 1.5 points on the 10-point scale, we conclude T1 is more likely. frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment (e.g., market demand, competitive landscape, regulatory requirements, or existing consumer adoption).
Cannot rely on post‑2002 developments or later market outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., personal marine safety beacon for recreational boaters).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., sell existing 406 MHz beacons through retail channels to individual buyers).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military/commercial marine).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Form partnerships with consumer brands to co‑brand a consumer‑focused beacon.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon for recreational boating if they view it as a safety necessity that meets regulatory requirements, leading to demand for a differentiated product. This theory remains unproven by real evidence; the simulated result is excluded from evidence weighting.
T1.who_benefits: Recreational boaters seeking enhanced safety compliance and peace of mind.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory pressure (e.g., maritime safety rules) and media coverage of boating accidents make a certified beacon a required or strongly recommended item, shifting perception from optional luxury to essential safety gear.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge premium prices for a certified, differentiated beacon and capture value through direct-to-consumer sales and brand association with safety compliance.
assumptions: Regulatory requirements for recreational boats will continue to mandate or strongly recommend 406 MHz beacons.
Consumers are willing to pay premium prices for safety-certified equipment.
ACR's existing certification and reputation for reliability will transfer to consumer market.
predictions: Surveyed boaters will indicate intent to purchase a certified beacon if price is under $1,000.
Sales of ACR's consumer beacon will correlate with regions having stricter maritime safety regulations.

T2.claim: Individual consumers will purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon for recreational boating if they view it as a status symbol or fashion accessory, leading to demand for a differentiated, aesthetically designed product.
T2.who_benefits: Recreational boaters seeking to display safety compliance as a status marker and differentiate their vessels.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Media coverage of high-profile boating incidents and social influence among peer groups make safety equipment a visible marker of responsibility and status, shifting perception from purely functional to aspirational.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by offering limited-edition designs, premium finishes, and co-branding with lifestyle brands, commanding higher margins through perceived exclusivity.
assumptions: Consumers associate safety equipment with status and are willing to pay for design differentiation.
Social media and peer influence amplify the status value of visible safety gear.
ACR can successfully design and market aesthetically differentiated beacons.
predictions: Boaters will express willingness to purchase a beacon with unique design features even at higher price points.
Sales will be higher in markets where boating culture emphasizes lifestyle and status.

position.recommendation: Deere & Company should develop a differentiated consumer proposition for households with small gardens, leveraging its engineering and dealer network. The evidence indicates strong demand for garden tractors from this segment, driven by practicality and cost-effectiveness, while T2 lacks supporting evidence for commercial adoption as the primary driver.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, practical solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and its engineering expertise to differentiate from competitors.
assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.
Small garden owners prioritize cost-effectiveness and ease of use over brand prestige.
Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales of lawn and garden tractors will increase relative to competitors.
Surveyed small garden owners will indicate willingness to pay a premium for Deere's engineering and brand.
Deere's dealer network will report higher foot traffic and accessory sales from garden tractor buyers.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Commercial users require equipment that can handle continuous use and offers quick parts/service availability; Deere's reputation for robust engineering and dealer support makes it attractive.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price commercial tractors at a premium, sell service contracts, and increase attachment sales, capturing value through both equipment and ongoing service revenue.
assumptions: Commercial landscaping and small farm markets are growing in the 1960s.
Deere's dealer network provides adequate service coverage for commercial users.
Commercial buyers prioritize reliability and service over price.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated commercial garden tractor proposition, sales to professional landscapers will increase relative to competitors.
Commercial buyers will report higher satisfaction with Deere's service support compared to other brands.

X1.name: Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 households with small gardens (verified by self‑report of garden size <0.5 acre) and 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators (verified by self‑report of commercial use). Randomly assign each respondent to either a consumer‑focused message (emphasizing low cost, ease of use, and suitability for small gardens) or a commercial‑focused message (emphasizing durability, service support, and suitability for professional work). After exposure, ask: "How likely are you to purchase a John Deere garden tractor?" on a 1‑10 scale. Also ask: "What is the maximum price you would pay?" and "Would you recommend this to others in your segment?". The test will be run in 12 weeks with a €20,000 budget for platform fees, incentives, and data analysis.
X1.sample: 400 respondents (200 small‑garden households, 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators).
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each segment under each message condition.

final.recommendation: Deere & Company should develop a differentiated consumer proposition for households with small gardens, leveraging its existing dealer network and engineering expertise. The evidence indicates strong demand for garden tractors from this segment, driven by practicality and cost-effectiveness, while T2 lacks supporting evidence for commercial adoption as the primary driver.
final.target_customer: Households with small gardens (suburban homeowners)
final.value_proposition: A reliable, economical, and practical garden tractor that leverages Deere's engineering reputation for durability and ease of use, sold through the existing dealer network.
final.next_action: Launch a pilot production run of a differentiated garden tractor model (e.g., the 110 model) and test market response through the dealer network, focusing on suburban markets.
final.uncertainty: The exact price point and feature set that will resonate with suburban homeowners is not yet known; the dealer network's ability to effectively market to individual consumers without prior experience in this segment is uncertain.

arguments.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
arguments.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, practical solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and its engineering expertise to differentiate from competitors.
assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.
Small garden owners prioritize cost-effectiveness and ease of use over brand prestige.
Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales of lawn and garden tractors will increase relative to competitors.
Surveyed small garden owners will indicate willingness to pay a premium for Deere's engineering and brand.
Deere's dealer network will report higher foot traffic and accessory sales from garden tractor buyers.

arguments.claim: Professional landscapers and small farm operators will adopt garden tractors because they need reliable, efficient equipment for commercial work, and they value Deere's engineering reputation for durability and service support.
arguments.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by selling higher-margin commercial-grade tractors and attachments through its dealer network, leveraging its established service infrastructure.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Commercial users require equipment that can handle continuous use and offers quick parts/service availability; Deere's reputation for robust engineering and dealer support makes it attractive.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price commercial tractors at a premium, sell service contracts, and increase attachment sales, capturing value through both equipment and ongoing service revenue.
assumptions: Commercial landscaping and small farm markets are growing in the 1960s.
Deere's dealer network provides adequate service coverage for commercial users.
Commercial buyers prioritize reliability and service over price.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated commercial garden tractor proposition, sales to professional landscapers will increase relative to competitors.
Commercial buyers will report higher satisfaction with Deere's service support compared to other brands.
Deere's dealer network will see increased service contract uptake from commercial customers.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 households with small gardens (verified by self‑report of garden size <0.5 acre) and 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators (verified by self‑report of commercial use). Randomly assign each respondent to either a consumer‑focused message (emphasizing low cost, ease of use, and suitability for small gardens) or a commercial‑focused message (emphasizing durability, service support, and suitability for professional work). After exposure, ask: "How likely are you to purchase a John Deere garden tractor?" on a 1‑10 scale. Also ask: "What is the maximum price you would pay?" and "Would you recommend this to others in your segment?". The test will be run in 12 weeks with a €20,000 budget for platform fees, incentives, and data analysis.
arguments.sample: 400 respondents (200 small‑garden households, 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators).
arguments.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each segment under each message condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Households with small gardens will show higher purchase intent when exposed to the consumer message than when exposed to the commercial message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional landscapers/small farm operators will show higher purchase intent when exposed to the commercial message than when exposed to the consumer message.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two message conditions for households with small gardens is at least 1.5 points (on the 10‑point scale) and the difference for professionals is at least 1.5 points in the opposite direction, then both theories are supported and the test is inconclusive for a single recommendation. arguments.uncertainty: The exact price point and feature set that will resonate with suburban homeowners is not yet known; the dealer network's ability to effectively market to individual consumers without prior experience in this segment is uncertain.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, practical solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and its engineering expertise to differentiate from competitors.
assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.
Small garden owners prioritize cost-effectiveness and ease of use over brand prestige.
Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales of lawn and garden tractors will increase relative to competitors.
Surveyed small garden owners will indicate willingness to pay a premium for Deere's engineering and brand.
Deere's dealer network will report higher foot traffic and accessory sales from garden tractor buyers.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. This demand is driven by rising homeownership rates and the practical utility of garden tractors for yard work, not by Deere's existing product line or dealer network capabilities.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing consumer sales through its existing dealer network and by leveraging its engineering to produce a differentiated garden tractor.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership rates in the 1950s-1960s increase the number of households with small gardens. These households seek practical, low‑maintenance solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need at an affordable price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell garden tractors through its independent dealer network, using the same engineering platform as farm tractors but scaled down. The value is captured through direct sales revenue and increased dealer traffic.
assumptions: Homeownership trends continue to rise, providing a growing base of potential buyers.
Garden tractors remain inexpensive and practical compared to manual tools.
Deere's dealer network can effectively reach individual homeowners.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor, sales will be positively correlated with regional homeownership rates.
Consumer surveys will show that price sensitivity and ease of use are primary purchase drivers for garden tractors.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.

T2.claim: Small‑farm operators will adopt a differentiated tractor proposition because they need a versatile, affordable machine that can replace multiple tools and reduce labor costs, and Deere can capture value by selling through its dealer network and offering financing.
T2.who_benefits: Deere & Company benefits by expanding its market beyond large farms to smallholders, increasing sales volume and dealer engagement.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Post‑war agricultural mechanization and rising labor costs make small farms seek equipment that can perform multiple tasks (plowing, planting, hauling) without requiring a large crew. A tractor that is cheaper than a full‑size farm tractor
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price a small‑farm tractor below its standard farm models, sell it through existing dealers, and offer financing to lower the entry barrier. Value is captured through higher unit volume and increased dealer traffic.
assumptions: Small farms constitute a sizable segment with unmet equipment needs.
Labor costs are rising enough to justify mechanization.
Deere's dealer network can reach small‑farm owners.
predictions: Sales of a differentiated small‑farm tractor will be higher in regions with a higher proportion of farms under 100 acres.
Purchasers will cite labor cost savings and task versatility as primary reasons for buying.
